blocks.title: Academic Passage 1
blocks.passage:
In 1968, ecologist Garrett Hardin popularized the phrase "the tragedy of the commons" to describe a situation in which individuals, acting in their own interest, deplete a shared resource. His classic example was a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains by adding one more animal, yet the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the incentive to add animals always outweighs the incentive to restrain.

Hardin concluded that shared resources inevitably collapse unless access is limited by private ownership or government regulation. Later research, however, challenged this pessimism. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom documented communities in Switzerland, Japan, and the Philippines that had managed forests and irrigation systems collectively for centuries. Their success depended on clear boundaries, local monitoring, and rules that members themselves created and enforced.

options: A debate over whether shared resources inevitably collapse

items.q: The word "deplete" is closest in meaning to

options: They gain individually while the cost is shared
items.explain: La ganancia es individual; el costo, colectivo.

items.q: Why does the author mention Switzerland, Japan and the Philippines?
options: To show real communities that managed shared resources successfully
items.explain: Son ejemplos de gestión colectiva exitosa.

blocks.title: Academic Passage 2
blocks.passage:
Concrete is the most widely used construction material on Earth, but its production is carbon-intensive. Roughly eight percent of global carbon dioxide emissions come from cement, the binding ingredient, because making it requires heating limestone to extremely high temperatures, which releases the gas stored in the rock.

Engineers are exploring alternatives. Some replace part of the cement with industrial by-products such as fly ash, which reduces emissions without weakening the final product. Others experiment with "self-healing" concrete containing bacteria that produce limestone when cracks form, extending a structure's lifespan. A third approach captures carbon dioxide and injects it into the mixture, where it becomes permanently mineralized.

Although these technologies are promising, adoption is slow, partly because building codes are conservative and partly because the cheapest cement remains the traditional kind.

items.q: Why does making cement release carbon dioxide?
options: Limestone is heated and releases stored gas
items.explain: El calentamiento de la caliza libera CO₂.

segments.text: Let's consider why some words enter a language and others disappear. Linguists call the process lexical change. One major driver is technology. When smartphones appeared, we needed words like 'selfie' and 'texting', and they spread within a few years.

Another driver is social attitudes. Terms considered acceptable decades ago may now sound offensive, so speakers abandon them. Meanwhile, words can change meaning. 'Awful' once meant 'inspiring awe', but today it means 'very bad'.

Here's the interesting part. Dictionary editors don't decide which words are legitimate. They record what speakers actually use. So if a word appears frequently across many sources over a period of time, it earns a place. In other words, language belongs to its users.

options: It changed from "inspiring awe" to "very bad"

segments.text: Today we turn to a famous problem in psychology: why do groups sometimes make worse decisions than individuals? One reason is groupthink, a term coined by Irving Janis in the 1970s. Groupthink occurs when members value harmony so highly that they stop questioning the leader's ideas.

A classic case is the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, planned by a close-knit advisory team. Later analysis showed that several advisors had doubts but kept quiet to avoid disrupting consensus. The plan failed badly.

How can groups avoid this trap? Janis recommended assigning one member the role of devil's advocate, and inviting outsiders to criticize the plan. Interestingly, studies show that groups with a designated critic reach better decisions, even when the critic's role is only symbolic.

items.q: What is the main topic of the talk?
options: Groupthink and how to avoid it

items.q: Why does the professor discuss the Bay of Pigs?
options: To provide an example of groupthink

items.q: What did Janis recommend?
options: Assign a devil's advocate and invite outsiders

items.q: What can be inferred from the final study mentioned?
options: Even a symbolic critic can improve decisions

blocks.title: Write an Email
blocks.prompt:
**Situation.** You are a member of the university hiking club. The trip planned for Saturday must be cancelled because of a weather warning, and some members have already paid.

**Write an email to all club members.** In your email:
- Announce the cancellation and explain the reason.
- Describe how refunds or a new date will be handled.
- Invite members to share their preferences.
blocks.model:
Dear club members,

I am sorry to announce that Saturday's hiking trip has been cancelled. The weather service has issued a storm warning for the mountain area, and we cannot risk anyone's safety.

Those who have already paid will receive a full refund within a week, unless they prefer to keep their payment for a new date. We are considering Saturday, November 14 as a replacement.

Please let me know by Wednesday whether that date suits you, or suggest another weekend. Your preferences will help us decide.

Thank you for your understanding.

Best wishes,
Irene, Hiking Club Coordinator

blocks.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
blocks.prompt:
**Professor Adler:** Many cities are replacing paper tickets and cash with digital payment systems. Do you think this change is beneficial overall?

**Leo:** Yes. Digital payments are faster, cheaper to manage, and reduce crime related to cash.

**Mia:** I disagree. Not everyone has a smartphone or a bank account, and these systems can exclude older people and the poor.

**Write a response** (≥ 110 words) giving your opinion, acknowledging the other side, and supporting your view with an example.
blocks.model:
I think digital payments are largely beneficial, but cities must protect those who cannot use them. Leo is right that digital systems are efficient. For example, when Stockholm introduced card-only buses, boarding became noticeably faster and operators saved on cash handling.

Admittedly, Mia raises an important concern about exclusion. Nevertheless, this risk can be reduced if governments keep cash options, provide prepaid cards for those without bank accounts, and offer assistance to older users.

Overall, a gradual, inclusive transition would deliver the advantages of digital payments without leaving anyone behind.

questions.q: What motivates you to keep working when a task becomes difficult?

segments.text: What motivates you to keep working when a task becomes difficult?

questions.model: What motivates me is the idea of seeing a result. When a task becomes difficult, I divide it into small steps and celebrate each one. For example, when I wrote my thesis proposal, I set a goal of two pages a day, and that made the whole project manageable.

questions.q: How do you think technology will change education in the next ten years?

segments.text: How do you think technology will change education in the next ten years?

questions.model: I think technology will personalize education. Software will adapt exercises to each student's level, and teachers will focus on discussion and mentoring. For instance, language apps already adjust difficulty in real time, and this will become common in many subjects.

questions.q: Describe a skill you have that you think is useful for university study.

segments.text: Describe a skill you have that you think is useful for university study.

questions.model: I think my ability to organize information is very useful. I make summaries and diagrams of every topic, so I can review quickly. For example, during my last exam period, my diagrams helped me recall three chapters in a single evening.

questions.q: Do you think students should be graded on effort or on results? Explain.

segments.text: Do you think students should be graded on effort or on results? Explain.

questions.model: I think results should matter most, but effort deserves some recognition. Results show whether learning actually occurred, whereas effort is hard to measure. For example, a student may study many hours with the wrong method, so the grade should reflect the outcome, perhaps with a small bonus for participation.
